children: Oil prices rose Wednesday, with Brent crude recovering above $92 a barrel after a sharp selloff, as renewed strikes in the region tempered expectations of a diplomatic resolution to the U.S.-Iran conflict.
Front-month Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, rose 1.2% to $92.55 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate futures gained 0.7% to $86.67 a barrel.

The gains followed several sessions of steep declines after President Trump signaled that further U.S. military action against Iran was unlikely for now, raising hopes that negotiations could bring an end to the conflict.

In recent days, the U.S. has repeatedly struck Iran's Qeshm Island, which houses Revolutionary Guard missile and drone facilities, while Tehran said Tuesday it targeted an Omani island used to help ships navigate the Strait of Hormuz, The Wall Street Journal reported. U.S. and Gulf officials described the American strikes as defensive operations aimed at protecting commercial shipping rather than preparations for a broader military offensive.

The recent selloff might have less room to run without further progress in negotiations, according to Scott Shelton of TP ICAP. Speculative long positions held by commodity trading advisers have largely been unwound, potentially reducing the selling pressure that has weighed on oil futures in recent sessions, he said in a note.

MUFG said the recent decline in oil prices could prove difficult to sustain without a lasting diplomatic settlement and greater confidence among shipping companies that vessels can safely transit the waterway. The bank noted that an earlier agreement to reopen the strait lasted only a few weeks before attacks resumed.

Meanwhile, physical oil markets are showing signs of excess supply in some regions. Physical Brent crude fell to its weakest level against futures in about five months, as elevated freight costs and cheaper Middle Eastern barrels limited demand for North Sea crude in Asia, according to S&P Global Commodity Insights.
The physical Brent discount to futures reached $2.12 a barrel Monday, S&P Global said, while several North Sea cargoes remained without buyers.
